Lessons.Title: Growing and Growing
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: explore and compare repeated addition with repeated multiplication through tables and graphs, predict when a rapidly multiplying amount overtakes a larger but steadily increasing one, and describe reasoning before formal function labels. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/1/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/1/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source juxtaposes bacterial multiplication and competing offers; our data are independently chosen, not verified biology or finance.

Original fictional two reward schemes for whole weeks t≥0: Plan A begins at100 tokens and adds30 each week, A(t)=100+30t; Plan B begins at10 and doubles each week, B(t)=10×2^t. At t=0 A100 vs B10, t=1 A130 vs B20, t=2 A160 vs B40, t=3 A190 vs B80, t=4 A220 vs B160 and t=5 A250 vs B320. The multiplication plan first overtakes the additive plan at whole week5.

An additive pattern has a constant increase (+30 each step); a multiplying pattern has a constant ratio (×2 each step), which produces progressively larger differences. Drawing points on common axes should preserve the rapid growth. Do not assert an infinitely sustainable real-world token economy from invented examples.

Student task: continue both tables to week7 by reasoning and optional spreadsheet, sketch and compare graphs, support when Plan B first surpasses Plan A with adjacent-week checks, then design a third plan that changes the crossing week. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for valid tables, structural pattern explanation, correct overtaking point, and critique of changed assumptions and graph scales.

V12 source-aligned original tripling sequence for the activity paralleling bacteria reproduction: start with ONE fictional microscopic object and triple each step. Counts at steps0,1,2,3,4 are1,3,9,27,81. Students draw the objects for steps0 through3, write repeated multiplication 3×3×3=27, and explain why "add three" cannot produce the same sequence. This is not a verified physical observation.

V12 original comparison activity: construct a table for the existing fictional reward schemes A(t)=100+30t and B(t)=10×2^t at whole weeks0..6. On the same labeled axes plot both curves, identify week5 as the first integer week when B>A, and explain why constant additive differences and constant multiplicative factors lead to different predictions. Students may independently use a scientific calculator or spreadsheet but must record actual tool use; no claim of a performed spreadsheet interaction appears in this lesson.

Draft teacher criteria0–2 each for correct diagrams/3^t counts, both exact schemes through week6, genuine two-curve plotted graph with correct intersection ordering, and justified comparisons plus conditional technology report. Graph reading and learner-generated plotting remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated addition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quantity changes by a fixed difference each equal step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each new output is a fixed multiple of the preceding one.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply by common factor b for each step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Crossover reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare values at the same input, including adjacent integer steps.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Verify when one first exceeds another in the stated domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Continue additive versus doubling
WorkedExamples.Question: Find A(t), B(t) at t=3,4,5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: The doubling plan crosses above between integer weeks4 and5.
WorkedExamples.Answer: At week5 Plan B320 exceeds A250.
WorkedExamples.Check: The stated domain is nonnegative whole weeks.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain different structures
WorkedExamples.Question: For A and B above, compare consecutive changes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: A difference A(t+1)−A(t)=30 for all t.
B ratio B(t+1)/B(t)=2 for all t.
B differences grow from10 to20 to40 to80...
Constant multiplier is not the same as constant difference.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A has fixed addition30; B fixed ratio2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict later amounts
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare plans at week7.
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: The multiplicative pattern dominates by that time.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating doubling as adding the starting value each week
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This would be linear, not repeated multiplication.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply the current value by2 each step.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming first crossover merely from t5 comparison
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One needs to rule out earlier integer weeks.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check all earlier table rows or prove pattern difference.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Plotting the two plans on different scales

SummaryPoints: Fixed differences and fixed ratios produce different growth patterns.
A starts larger but B's multiplier eventually dominates.
In the fictional plans, B first overtakes A at week5.
Teacher reviews tables, comparisons and source-specific reasoning.
